captions.instagram:
How does film editing work?

Three cameras filmed the same café scene. Cut it yourself on a live timeline, drag a cut on an opening door until it jumps, put the same blank face next to soup or a coffin, and speed a scene up from 10-second shots to 1.5.

→ Three cameras filmed the same moment. The editor picks which one you see.
→ A cut takes no time at all, and it hides best when a new person starts to speak.
→ Cut in the middle of a movement and the eye follows it straight across the cut.
→ Cross the 180-degree line and two people who face each other seem to look away.
→ The same blank face, cut next to a bowl of soup: viewers say he looks hungry.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/editclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does film editing work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Three cameras filmed the same café scene. Cut it yourself on a live timeline, drag a cut on an opening door until it jumps, put the same blank face next to soup or a coffin, and speed a scene up from 10-second shots to 1.5.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/editclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/editclear

In this video:
• Choosing what you see. A scene is filmed from several set-ups, like a wide shot and two close-ups.
• Hiding the cut. Continuity editing keeps time and space flowing: cut in the middle of a movement, show someone looking and then what they see, match shapes, keep cameras on one side of the 180° line.
• Meaning from the join. In Kuleshov's famous experiment the same blank face seemed hungry next to soup and grieving next to a coffin.
• Pace and sound. Hollywood's average shot fell from about 10.5 seconds (1930 to 1955) to about 4.3 seconds (1990 to 2015), and many action films cut every 2 to 4 seconds.
• Transitions. Most joins are cuts, so the rarer transitions carry a message.
• From dailies to picture lock. Editors watch the dailies, build an assembly, then a rough and a fine cut until picture lock.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
